passage:
For a while I kept a little ledger in my head: who paid for dinner, who replied first, who owed whom. I'd sulk when a favour wasn't repaid, though I never said so.

The week my thesis draft was torn apart by my guide, I stopped counting. Samir turned up at ten at night with a tiffin of dal and rice and asked nothing. He sat on my floor proofreading references until past midnight, humming quietly, and didn't leave until they were done.

The next evening I said, "Thank you for the tiffin, and for staying until the references were finished. That was what got me through." I saw his ears go pink.

Two weeks later, when his cousin's engagement had him frazzled, I was the one at his door, with tea. Kunal, I thought, this is the part I wasn't doing.

qa.q: What did Samir bring at ten at night?
qa.a: He brought a tiffin of dal and rice.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt as Samir quietly proofread on the floor?
qa.a: Kunal likely felt grateful and a little uncomfortable, since Samir's help was not something to tally and the old habit of counting favours and sulking suddenly looked petty.

qa.q: What could Kunal do beyond saying thank you?
qa.a: Show up for Samir in his own hard week, as Kunal did with the tea, without expecting a matching favour back.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt on hearing Kunal's specific thanks?
qa.a: He probably felt seen, since he learned exactly which part of his quiet effort mattered, which fits the pink ears.

grounding: Shows noticing a partner's quiet support, thanking specifically and reciprocating instead of scorekeeping.
